lessons.body:
## Boundaries before code

A data-table app has natural seams: the **data client** (fetch/cache/dedupe), the **view logic** (filter/sort/search as pure functions), the **table** (presentational: props in, callbacks out), the **detail view**, and the **wiring** (state ownership + effects). Give each seam its own module. Feature-first folders beat type-first folders here: `employees/api.js`, `employees/filters.js`, `employees/DataTable.jsx`, `employees/DetailPanel.jsx` — everything about one feature lives together.

## Where each piece of state lives

- **URL / shareable:** query, role filter, sort column + direction. (In this capstone we keep them in state for focus, but know the production move is query params.)
- **Component state:** the selected row id, panel open/closed, form drafts.
- **Cache:** the server rows, owned by the data client — never copied into component state per view.
- **Derived, never stored:** the filtered/sorted rows are computed with `useMemo` from rows + filter state. Storing them would be the derived-state trap from the state module.

## Data flows down, events flow up

`App` owns the state and passes data down; `DataTable` calls back up (`onSort`, `onSelect`). The table never fetches, never filters — it renders what it is given. That separation is what makes the table testable and reusable.
keyPoints: One feature, one folder: data client, view logic, table, detail view, wiring.
Shareable UI state leans toward the URL; selection and drafts stay local; server rows live in the cache.
Filtered/sorted rows are derived with useMemo — never stored.
Presentational components take props and emit callbacks; they never fetch.
lessons.title: App Architecture: Boundaries and State Placement

lessons.body:
## The four states (not two)

Loading and error are the obvious ones. The two teams forget are **empty** (the dataset itself is empty) and **no-results** (filters match nothing). They need different copy and different actions — no-results wants a "clear filters" button, empty wants an invitation to add data.

## Fetch once, share everywhere

The data client dedupes in-flight requests: if the table and the detail view both ask for `/employees`, one network request serves both. Responses are cached with a TTL so back-navigation is instant, and stale-while-revalidate keeps them fresh without blocking the UI.

## Loading UX that respects the user

Skeleton rows beat spinners for tables: they hold the layout steady (no content jump) and communicate *shape*, not just *waiting*. Mark the region `aria-busy` so assistive tech announces the state instead of silence. Reserve spinners for actions, not page loads.

## Errors with a way out

Every error state needs three things: what happened (plain language), what the user can do (retry button), and the `role="alert"` semantics so it is announced. A dead-end error message is a bug, not a state.
keyPoints: Design four states: loading, error, empty, and no-results — each with its own copy and action.
Dedupe in-flight requests so parallel components share one network call.
Cache with TTL for instant back-navigation; revalidate stale data in the background.
Skeleton rows hold layout steady and announce via aria-busy; spinners are for actions.
lessons.title: The Data Layer: Fetch, Cache, and the Empty States

lessons.body:
## Tables are already semantic — keep them that way

Use the real elements: `<table>`, `<th scope="col">`, `<td>`. A div-grid that looks like a table is invisible to assistive tech. The sorted column gets `aria-sort` so the sort state is perceivable without seeing the arrow glyph.

## Controls must be controls

Sortable headers are `<button>` elements, not clickable divs — keyboard focus and activation come free. Every input has a label. If you can operate the whole table without a mouse, you are most of the way there.

## The dialog contract

Opening the detail view must: move focus into it, trap the Escape key to close, and return focus to the invoking row on close. `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal` + a labelled heading tells assistive tech what just happened. The cleanup function is where this lives or dies — remove the listener, restore the focus.

## Keyboard-operable rows

Rows that open a detail view must be reachable and activatable by keyboard (Enter/Space on a focusable row, or an explicit "view" button per row). Visible focus styles are non-negotiable — if you cannot see where focus is, keyboard users are lost.
keyPoints: Real table elements + th scope + aria-sort; never a div-grid lookalike.
Sortable headers are buttons; every input has a label.
Dialog: focus in on open, Escape closes, focus restored on close, listener cleaned up.
Rows activatable by keyboard with visible focus styles.
lessons.title: Polish: Accessibility and Keyboard UX
